P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

In △DEF, ∠E=90°\angle E = 90°∠E=90°, DE = 33 cm, EF = 56 cm and DF = 65 cm. The value of tan⁡F\tan FtanF is:

tan⁡=oppositeadjacent\tan = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}tan=adjacentopposite​, with sides labelled from ∠F\angle F∠F (Topic 1). Why it applies: the question asks about F, not D.

This is EFDE\dfrac{EF}{DE}DEEF​ — opposite and adjacent swapped (it is tan⁡D\tan DtanD).
From F, the opposite side is DE = 33 and the adjacent side is EF = 56, so tan⁡F=3356\tan F = \dfrac{33}{56}tanF=5633​.
This is DEDF\dfrac{DE}{DF}DFDE​, which is sin⁡F\sin FsinF.
This is EFDF\dfrac{EF}{DF}DFEF​, which is cos⁡F\cos FcosF.

Given: the three sides; right angle at E. Asked: tan⁡F\tan FtanF.

Concept used: tan⁡=oppositeadjacent\tan = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}tan=adjacentopposite​, with sides labelled from ∠F\angle F∠F (Topic 1). Why it applies: the question asks about F, not D.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ This is EFDE\dfrac{EF}{DE}DEEF​ — opposite and adjacent swapped (it is tan⁡D\tan DtanD).
    • (b) ✔ From F, the opposite side is DE = 33 and the adjacent side is EF = 56, so tan⁡F=3356\tan F = \dfrac{33}{56}tanF=5633​.
    • (c) ✘ This is DEDF\dfrac{DE}{DF}DFDE​, which is sin⁡F\sin FsinF.
    • (d) ✘ This is EFDF\dfrac{EF}{DF}DFEF​, which is cos⁡F\cos FcosF.

  2. Check: 332+562=1089+3136=4225=65233^2 + 56^2 = 1089 + 3136 = 4225 = 65^2332+562=1089+3136=4225=652 ✔.

  3. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Labelling from D. Mark angle F with an arc before you write anything — opposite/adjacent swaps are one of the most common mistakes in this chapter.
P2● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

In △ABC, ∠C=90°\angle C = 90°∠C=90°. Then cosec⁡A\operatorname{cosec} AcosecA is equal to:

cosec⁡A=hypotenuseopposite\operatorname{cosec} A = \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{opposite}}cosecA=oppositehypotenuse​ (Topic 1). Why it applies: label from A: hypotenuse AB (opposite the right angle at C), opposite BC, adjacent AC.

hypopp=ABBC\dfrac{\text{hyp}}{\text{opp}} = \dfrac{AB}{BC}opphyp​=BCAB​.
ABAC=hypadj=sec⁡A\dfrac{AB}{AC} = \dfrac{\text{hyp}}{\text{adj}} = \sec AACAB​=adjhyp​=secA — the sec/cosec mix-up.
BCAB=sin⁡A\dfrac{BC}{AB} = \sin AABBC​=sinA — not flipped.
ACBC=adjopp=cot⁡A\dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{opp}} = \cot ABCAC​=oppadj​=cotA.

Given: right angle at C. Asked: cosec⁡A\operatorname{cosec} AcosecA in terms of the sides.

Concept used: cosec⁡A=hypotenuseopposite\operatorname{cosec} A = \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{opposite}}cosecA=oppositehypotenuse​ (Topic 1). Why it applies: label from A: hypotenuse AB (opposite the right angle at C), opposite BC, adjacent AC.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ hypopp=ABBC\dfrac{\text{hyp}}{\text{opp}} = \dfrac{AB}{BC}opphyp​=BCAB​.
    • (b) ✘ ABAC=hypadj=sec⁡A\dfrac{AB}{AC} = \dfrac{\text{hyp}}{\text{adj}} = \sec AACAB​=adjhyp​=secA — the sec/cosec mix-up.
    • (c) ✘ BCAB=sin⁡A\dfrac{BC}{AB} = \sin AABBC​=sinA — not flipped.
    • (d) ✘ ACBC=adjopp=cot⁡A\dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{opp}} = \cot ABCAC​=oppadj​=cotA.

  2. Check: cosec⁡A×sin⁡A=ABBC×BCAB=1\operatorname{cosec} A \times \sin A = \dfrac{AB}{BC} \times \dfrac{BC}{AB} = 1cosecA×sinA=BCAB​×ABBC​=1 ✔.

  3. Answer (a)

    Common trap: Taking the hypotenuse as AC because "C is the right angle". The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, AB.
P3● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

In △ABC, right-angled at B, AB = 16 cm and AC = 34 cm. Find sin⁡A\sin AsinA and cos⁡A\cos AcosA.

Full solution

Given: AB = 16 cm, AC = 34 cm, ∠B=90°\angle B = 90°∠B=90°. Asked: sin⁡A\sin AsinA, cos⁡A\cos AcosA.

Concept used: Pythagoras for BC; then SOH-CAH-TOA from ∠A\angle A∠A (Topics 1–2). Why it applies: sin⁡A\sin AsinA needs the opposite side BC.

  1. 1

    AC is the hypotenuse. BC is a shorter side, so subtract.

    BC2=342−162=1156−256BC^2 = 34^2 - 16^2 = 1156 - 256BC2=342−162=1156−256Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Subtract.

    BC2=900BC^2 = 900BC2=900Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Take the square root.

    BC=30 cmBC = 30 \text{ cm}BC=30 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    From ∠A\angle A∠A: opposite BC = 30, adjacent AB = 16, hypotenuse AC = 34.

    sin⁡A=3034=1517,cos⁡A=1634=817\sin A = \dfrac{30}{34} = \dfrac{15}{17}, \qquad \cos A = \dfrac{16}{34} = \dfrac{8}{17}sinA=3430​=1715​,cosA=3416​=178​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: (1517)2+(817)2=225+64289=1\left(\dfrac{15}{17}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{8}{17}\right)^2 = \dfrac{225 + 64}{289} = 1(1715​)2+(178​)2=289225+64​=1 ✔.

  6. Answer sin⁡A=1517\sin A = \dfrac{15}{17}sinA=1715​, cos⁡A=817\cos A = \dfrac{8}{17}cosA=178​

    Common trap: sin⁡A=1634\sin A = \dfrac{16}{34}sinA=3416​ — using AB (which touches A) as the opposite side.

the table (Topic 4). Why it applies: both angles are standard.

As above.

Uses tan⁡30°=13\tan 30° = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tan30°=3​1​ in place of tan⁡60°\tan 60°tan60°: 32×13\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}23​​×3​1​.
Swaps both 30° and 60°: cos⁡60°×tan⁡30°\cos 60° \times \tan 30°cos60°×tan30°.

Given: an expression in table values. Asked: its value.

Concept used: the table (Topic 4). Why it applies: both angles are standard.

  1. 1

    cos⁡30°=32\cos 30° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}cos30°=23​​ and tan⁡60°=3\tan 60° = \sqrt{3}tan60°=3​.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ As above.
    • (b) ✘ Uses cos⁡60°=12\cos 60° = \dfrac{1}{2}cos60°=21​ in place of cos⁡30°\cos 30°cos30°: 12×3\dfrac{1}{2} \times \sqrt{3}21​×3​.
    • (c) ✘ Uses tan⁡30°=13\tan 30° = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}tan30°=3​1​ in place of tan⁡60°\tan 60°tan60°: 32×13\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}23​​×3​1​.

P5● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Evaluate 4cos⁡260°+3sec⁡230°−2tan⁡245°4\cos^2 60° + 3\sec^2 30° - 2\tan^2 45°4cos260°+3sec230°−2tan245°.

Full solution

Given: an expression with squared table values. Asked: its value.

Concept used: square each value (top and bottom), multiply, then add/subtract (Topic 4). Why it applies: all angles are in the table.

  1. 1

    Square the values.

    cos⁡260°=14,sec⁡230°=(23)2=43,tan⁡245°=1\cos^2 60° = \dfrac{1}{4}, \qquad \sec^2 30° = \left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{3}, \qquad \tan^2 45° = 1cos260°=41​,sec230°=(3​2​)2=34​,tan245°=1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Substitute.

    4×14+3×43−2×14 \times \dfrac{1}{4} + 3 \times \dfrac{4}{3} - 2 \times 14×41​+3×34​−2×1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Multiply.

    =1+4−2= 1 + 4 - 2=1+4−2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Simplify.

    =3= 3=3Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: decimals: 4×0.25+3×1.3333−2=3.0004 \times 0.25 + 3 \times 1.3333 - 2 = 3.0004×0.25+3×1.3333−2=3.000 ✔.

  6. Answer 333

    Common trap: sec⁡230°=43\sec^2 30° = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}}sec230°=3​4​ — the bottom must be squared too.

P6● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

Write the values of (a) sin⁡90°\sin 90°sin90° (b) cot⁡90°\cot 90°cot90° (c) tan⁡90°\tan 90°tan90°.

Full solution

Given: three ratios of 90°. Asked: their values.

Concept used: at 90°, sin⁡=1\sin = 1sin=1 and cos⁡=0\cos = 0cos=0; tan and cot are quotients of these (Topic 4). Why it applies: a quotient with 0 on the bottom is not defined.

  1. 1

    (a) sin⁡90°=1\sin 90° = 1sin90°=1.

  2. 2

    (b) cot⁡90°=cos⁡90°sin⁡90°=01=0\cot 90° = \dfrac{\cos 90°}{\sin 90°} = \dfrac{0}{1} = 0cot90°=sin90°cos90°​=10​=0.

  3. 3

    (c) tan⁡90°=sin⁡90°cos⁡90°=10\tan 90° = \dfrac{\sin 90°}{\cos 90°} = \dfrac{1}{0}tan90°=cos90°sin90°​=01​, which is not defined.

  4. Check: cot 90° and tan 90° are reciprocals, and the reciprocal of 0 is not defined ✔.

  5. Answer (a) 111 (b) 000 (c) not defined

    Common trap: Writing tan⁡90°=0\tan 90° = 0tan90°=0 and cot⁡90°=\cot 90° =cot90°= not defined — the two are the other way round.

P7● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

If sin⁡A=0.6\sin A = 0.6sinA=0.6 and A is acute, then cos⁡A\cos AcosA is:

cos⁡2A=1−sin⁡2A\cos^2 A = 1 - \sin^2 Acos2A=1−sin2A; positive root for acute A (Topic 5). Why it applies: the identity links sin to cos directly.

Uses "sin⁡A+cos⁡A=1\sin A + \cos A = 1sinA+cosA=1", which is not an identity.
As above.
Stops at cos⁡2A\cos^2 Acos2A — forgot the square root.
Takes 1−0.6\sqrt{1 - 0.6}1−0.6​: subtracts sin instead of sin².

Given: sin⁡A=0.6\sin A = 0.6sinA=0.6. Asked: cos⁡A\cos AcosA.

Concept used: cos⁡2A=1−sin⁡2A\cos^2 A = 1 - \sin^2 Acos2A=1−sin2A; positive root for acute A (Topic 5). Why it applies: the identity links sin to cos directly.

  1. 1

    sin⁡2A=0.36\sin^2 A = 0.36sin2A=0.36.

  2. 2

    cos⁡2A=1−0.36=0.64\cos^2 A = 1 - 0.36 = 0.64cos2A=1−0.36=0.64.

  3. 3

    cos⁡A=0.64=0.8\cos A = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8cosA=0.64​=0.8.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Uses "sin⁡A+cos⁡A=1\sin A + \cos A = 1sinA+cosA=1", which is not an identity.
    • (b) ✔ As above.
    • (c) ✘ Stops at cos⁡2A\cos^2 Acos2A — forgot the square root.
    • (d) ✘ Takes 1−0.6\sqrt{1 - 0.6}1−0.6​: subtracts sin instead of sin².

  4. Check: 0.62+0.82=0.36+0.64=10.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 10.62+0.82=0.36+0.64=1 ✔.

  5. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Misusing the identity — option (a). Only the squares add to 1.
P8● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

Find the value of 5sec⁡2θ−5tan⁡2θ+25\sec^2\theta - 5\tan^2\theta + 25sec2θ−5tan2θ+2.

Full solution

Concept used: sec⁡2θ−tan⁡2θ=1\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1sec2θ−tan2θ=1 (Topic 5). Why it applies: the first two terms share the factor 5.

  1. 1

    Take out 5 from the first two terms.

    5(sec⁡2θ−tan⁡2θ)+25(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta) + 25(sec2θ−tan2θ)+2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Use sec⁡2θ−tan⁡2θ=1\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1sec2θ−tan2θ=1.

    =5×1+2= 5 \times 1 + 2=5×1+2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Simplify.

    =7= 7=7Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: at θ = 60°: 5×4−5×3+2=75 \times 4 - 5 \times 3 + 2 = 75×4−5×3+2=7 ✔.

P9● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which is a correct way to begin a proof of tan⁡Acos⁡A=sin⁡A\tan A \cos A = \sin AtanAcosA=sinA?

the proof layout — one side, changed line by line, until it becomes the other side (Topic 6). Why it applies: the question is about how a proof is written.

Starts from one side and makes one change (Move 1). The next line, =sin⁡A=RHS= \sin A = \text{RHS}=sinA=RHS, finishes it.
Writes the identity first and works on both sides — it assumes what is to be proved.
Changes both sides at once, as if solving an equation.
A check with one angle is evidence, not a proof.

Given: four starts. Asked: the correct one.

Concept used: the proof layout — one side, changed line by line, until it becomes the other side (Topic 6). Why it applies: the question is about how a proof is written.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ Starts from one side and makes one change (Move 1). The next line, =sin⁡A=RHS= \sin A = \text{RHS}=sinA=RHS, finishes it.
    • (b) ✘ Writes the identity first and works on both sides — it assumes what is to be proved.
    • (c) ✘ Changes both sides at once, as if solving an equation.
    • (d) ✘ A check with one angle is evidence, not a proof.

  2. Check: (a) continues as sin⁡Acos⁡A×cos⁡A=sin⁡A\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} \times \cos A = \sin AcosAsinA​×cosA=sinA ✔.

  3. Answer (a)

    Common trap: Thinking that ending with "sin⁡A=sin⁡A\sin A = \sin AsinA=sinA" proves something. It only shows that you assumed the result.
P10●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

If cot⁡θ=5633\cot\theta = \dfrac{56}{33}cotθ=3356​, find sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ and sec⁡θ\sec\thetasecθ.

Full solution

Given: cot⁡θ=5633\cot\theta = \dfrac{56}{33}cotθ=3356​. Asked: sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ, sec⁡θ\sec\thetasecθ.

Concept used: cot⁡=adjopp\cot = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{opp}}cot=oppadj​; five-step method (Topic 3). Why it applies: one ratio is given.

  1. 1

    Adjacent =56k= 56k=56k, opposite =33k= 33k=33k.

  2. 2

    Hypotenuse: add the squares.

    hyp2=3136k2+1089k2=4225k2\text{hyp}^2 = 3136k^2 + 1089k^2 = 4225k^2hyp2=3136k2+1089k2=4225k2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Take the square root.

    hyp=65k\text{hyp} = 65khyp=65kSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Sine and secant.

    sin⁡θ=3365,sec⁡θ=6556\sin\theta = \dfrac{33}{65}, \qquad \sec\theta = \dfrac{65}{56}sinθ=6533​,secθ=5665​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: sec⁡θ>1\sec\theta > 1secθ>1 and sin⁡θ<1\sin\theta < 1sinθ<1 ✔.

  6. Answer sin⁡θ=3365\sin\theta = \dfrac{33}{65}sinθ=6533​, sec⁡θ=6556\sec\theta = \dfrac{65}{56}secθ=5665​

    Common trap: Putting 56 on the opposite side (treating cot like tan), which gives sin⁡θ=5665\sin\theta = \dfrac{56}{65}sinθ=6556​.

Full solution

Given: tan⁡A=45\tan A = \dfrac{4}{5}tanA=54​. Asked: the value of the expression.

Concept used: divide the top and bottom by cos⁡A\cos AcosA to turn everything into tan⁡A\tan AtanA (Topic 3). Why it applies: every term on top and bottom has exactly one sin or cos.

    Divide every term on top and bottom by cos⁡A\cos AcosA (this does not change the value).

    5sin⁡Acos⁡A−35sin⁡Acos⁡A+2\dfrac{5\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} - 3}{5\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} + 2}5cosAsinA​+25cosAsinA​−3​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Replace sin⁡Acos⁡A\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A}cosAsinA​ by tan⁡A\tan AtanA.

    =5tan⁡A−35tan⁡A+2= \dfrac{5\tan A - 3}{5\tan A + 2}=5tanA+25tanA−3​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Substitute 5tan⁡A=45\tan A = 45tanA=4.

    =4−34+2= \dfrac{4 - 3}{4 + 2}=4+24−3​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Simplify.

    =16= \dfrac{1}{6}=61​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check (triangle route): opposite 4, adjacent 5, hypotenuse 41\sqrt{41}41​: 2041−15412041+1041=530=16\dfrac{\dfrac{20}{\sqrt{41}} - \dfrac{15}{\sqrt{41}}}{\dfrac{20}{\sqrt{41}} + \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{41}}} = \dfrac{5}{30} = \dfrac{1}{6}41​20​+41​10​41​20​−41​15​​=305​=61​ ✔.

  6. Answer 16\dfrac{1}{6}61​

    Common trap: Substituting tan⁡A=45\tan A = \dfrac{4}{5}tanA=54​ into 5tan⁡A5\tan A5tanA and then multiplying by 5 again.

    Top: tan⁡260°=3\tan^2 60° = 3tan260°=3, 4cos⁡245°=4×12=24\cos^2 45° = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 24cos245°=4×21​=2, 3sec⁡230°=3×43=43\sec^2 30° = 3 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 43sec230°=3×34​=4, 5cos⁡290°=05\cos^2 90° = 05cos290°=0.

    Top=3+2+4+0=9\text{Top} = 3 + 2 + 4 + 0 = 9Top=3+2+4+0=9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Bottom: cosec⁡30°=2\operatorname{cosec} 30° = 2cosec30°=2, sec⁡60°=2\sec 60° = 2sec60°=2, cot⁡230°=(3)2=3\cot^2 30° = (\sqrt{3})^2 = 3cot230°=(3​)2=3.

    Bottom=2+2−3=1\text{Bottom} = 2 + 2 - 3 = 1Bottom=2+2−3=1Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Divide.

    91=9\dfrac{9}{1} = 919​=9Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Common trap: Taking cos⁡90°=1\cos 90° = 1cos90°=1 (confusing it with cos⁡0°\cos 0°cos0°), which adds 5 to the top and gives 14.

Full solution

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: Move 4 (1−sin⁡2A=cos⁡2A1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A1−sin2A=cos2A) and the reciprocal sec⁡A=1cos⁡A\sec A = \dfrac{1}{\cos A}secA=cosA1​ (Topic 6). Why it applies: a 1-move proof.

  1. 1

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=sec⁡A (1−sin⁡2A)\text{LHS} = \sec A\,(1 - \sin^2 A)LHS=secA(1−sin2A)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Move 4: 1−sin⁡2A=cos⁡2A1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A1−sin2A=cos2A.

    =sec⁡Acos⁡2A= \sec A\cos^2 A=secAcos2ASwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    sec⁡A=1cos⁡A\sec A = \dfrac{1}{\cos A}secA=cosA1​.

    =1cos⁡A×cos⁡2A= \dfrac{1}{\cos A} \times \cos^2 A=cosA1​×cos2ASwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Cancel one cos⁡A\cos AcosA.

    =cos⁡A=RHS= \cos A = \text{RHS}=cosA=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Hence proved.

    Check: at A = 60°: 2×(1−34)=12=cos⁡60°2 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{3}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} = \cos 60°2×(1−43​)=21​=cos60° ✔.

    Common trap: Replacing 1−sin⁡2A1 - \sin^2 A1−sin2A by cos⁡A\cos AcosA (no square) — the "proof" then ends at sec⁡Acos⁡A=1\sec A\cos A = 1secAcosA=1, not cos⁡A\cos AcosA.

P20●● StandardProof · 2 marksOriginal

Prove that sin⁡θcosec⁡θ+cos⁡θsec⁡θ=1\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\operatorname{cosec}\theta} + \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sec\theta} = 1cosecθsinθ​+secθcosθ​=1.

Full solution

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: Move 1 (reciprocals), then Move 4 (sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1sin2θ+cos2θ=1). Why it applies: dividing by cosec is multiplying by sin.

  1. 1

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=sin⁡θcosec⁡θ+cos⁡θsec⁡θ\text{LHS} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\operatorname{cosec}\theta} + \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sec\theta}LHS=cosecθsinθ​+secθcosθ​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Dividing by cosec⁡θ=1sin⁡θ\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}cosecθ=sinθ1​ is multiplying by sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ; similarly for sec.

    =sin⁡θ×sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ×cos⁡θ= \sin\theta \times \sin\theta + \cos\theta \times \cos\theta=sinθ×sinθ+cosθ×cosθSwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Write as squares.

    =sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ= \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta=sin2θ+cos2θSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Move 4.

    =1=RHS= 1 = \text{RHS}=1=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

    Hence proved.

    Common trap: Writing sin⁡θcosec⁡θ=1\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\operatorname{cosec}\theta} = 1cosecθsinθ​=1 ("they are reciprocals"). Reciprocals multiply to 1; dividing one by the other gives sin⁡2θ\sin^2\thetasin2θ.

P21●● StandardProof · 3 marksOriginal

Prove that 11+cos⁡A+11−cos⁡A=2cosec⁡2A\dfrac{1}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1}{1 - \cos A} = 2\operatorname{cosec}^2 A1+cosA1​+1−cosA1​=2cosec2A.

Full solution

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: Move 2 (LCM), then Move 4 (1−cos⁡2A=sin⁡2A1 - \cos^2 A = \sin^2 A1−cos2A=sin2A). Why it applies: a 2-move proof — two fractions whose denominators multiply to 1−cos⁡2A1 - \cos^2 A1−cos2A.

  1. 1

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=11+cos⁡A+11−cos⁡A\text{LHS} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1}{1 - \cos A}LHS=1+cosA1​+1−cosA1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Move 2: LCM (1+cos⁡A)(1−cos⁡A)(1 + \cos A)(1 - \cos A)(1+cosA)(1−cosA).

    =(1−cos⁡A)+(1+cos⁡A)(1+cos⁡A)(1−cos⁡A)= \dfrac{(1 - \cos A) + (1 + \cos A)}{(1 + \cos A)(1 - \cos A)}=(1+cosA)(1−cosA)(1−cosA)+(1+cosA)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Simplify the top.

    =2(1+cos⁡A)(1−cos⁡A)= \dfrac{2}{(1 + \cos A)(1 - \cos A)}=(1+cosA)(1−cosA)2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Bottom: (a+b)(a−b)=a2−b2(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2(a+b)(a−b)=a2−b2.

    =21−cos⁡2A= \dfrac{2}{1 - \cos^2 A}=1−cos2A2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Move 4.

    =2sin⁡2A= \dfrac{2}{\sin^2 A}=sin2A2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Reciprocal.

    =2cosec⁡2A=RHS= 2\operatorname{cosec}^2 A = \text{RHS}=2cosec2A=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

    Hence proved.

    Common trap: Writing the bottom as 1−cos⁡A1 - \cos A1−cosA or 1+cos⁡2A1 + \cos^2 A1+cos2A. Use (a+b)(a−b)=a2−b2(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2(a+b)(a−b)=a2−b2.

P22●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Find the error in the proof

Ravi was asked to prove sec⁡2A+cosec⁡2A=sec⁡2Acosec⁡2A\sec^2 A + \operatorname{cosec}^2 A = \sec^2 A\operatorname{cosec}^2 Asec2A+cosec2A=sec2Acosec2A. He wrote:

sec⁡2A+cosec⁡2A=sec⁡2Acosec⁡2A\sec^2 A + \operatorname{cosec}^2 A = \sec^2 A\operatorname{cosec}^2 Asec2A+cosec2A=sec2Acosec2A
⇒sec⁡2A=sec⁡2Acosec⁡2A−cosec⁡2A\Rightarrow \sec^2 A = \sec^2 A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A - \operatorname{cosec}^2 A⇒sec2A=sec2Acosec2A−cosec2A
⇒sec⁡2A=cosec⁡2A(sec⁡2A−1)\Rightarrow \sec^2 A = \operatorname{cosec}^2 A(\sec^2 A - 1)⇒sec2A=cosec2A(sec2A−1)
⇒sec⁡2A=cosec⁡2Atan⁡2A=1sin⁡2A×sin⁡2Acos⁡2A=sec⁡2A\Rightarrow \sec^2 A = \operatorname{cosec}^2 A\tan^2 A = \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 A} \times \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\cos^2 A} = \sec^2 A⇒sec2A=cosec2Atan2A=sin2A1​×cos2Asin2A​=sec2A. Hence proved.

Explain what is wrong with his method, and write a correct proof.

Full solution

Given: Ravi's working. Asked: the error, and a correct proof.

Concept used: the proof layout (Topic 6); Moves 1, 2 and 4. Why it applies: every line of Ravi's algebra is true, but the method is not a proof.

  1. 1

    The error: Ravi began with the statement to be proved and "moved" cosec⁡2A\operatorname{cosec}^2 Acosec2A across the equals sign. That treats the identity as an equation already known to be true. A proof must start from one side and reach the other.

  2. 2

    Correct proof — start from the LHS.

    LHS=sec⁡2A+cosec⁡2A\text{LHS} = \sec^2 A + \operatorname{cosec}^2 ALHS=sec2A+cosec2ASwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Move 1.

    =1cos⁡2A+1sin⁡2A= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 A} + \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 A}=cos2A1​+sin2A1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Move 2: LCM sin⁡2Acos⁡2A\sin^2 A\cos^2 Asin2Acos2A.

    =sin⁡2A+cos⁡2Asin⁡2Acos⁡2A= \dfrac{\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A}{\sin^2 A\cos^2 A}=sin2Acos2Asin2A+cos2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Move 4.

    =1sin⁡2Acos⁡2A= \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 A\cos^2 A}=sin2Acos2A1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Split into two reciprocals.

    =1cos⁡2A×1sin⁡2A=sec⁡2Acosec⁡2A=RHS= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 A} \times \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 A} = \sec^2 A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A = \text{RHS}=cos2A1​×sin2A1​=sec2Acosec2A=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Hence proved.

    Check: at A = 45°: LHS =2+2=4= 2 + 2 = 4=2+2=4; RHS =2×2=4= 2 \times 2 = 4=2×2=4 ✔.

  8. Answer Error: he worked on both sides (moved terms across "="), assuming the result. Correct proof: steps 2–6.

    Common trap: Believing that reaching "sec⁡2A=sec⁡2A\sec^2 A = \sec^2 Asec2A=sec2A" proves the identity. It only shows that you started from it.

  2. 2

    So cos⁡A≠23\cos A \neq \dfrac{2}{3}cosA=32​. Use the identity correctly.

    Positive square root; 8=22\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}8​=22​.

    cos⁡A=223\cos A = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}cosA=322​​Swipe to see the whole equation →

P24●● StandardMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which of the following is not an identity (for acute A)?

the three identities and their rearranged forms (Topic 5). Why it applies: three options are rearrangements; one pairs the wrong ratios.

It is sin⁡2A+cos⁡2A=1\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1sin2A+cos2A=1 rearranged — an identity.
It is 1+tan⁡2A=sec⁡2A1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A1+tan2A=sec2A rearranged — an identity.
It is 1+cot⁡2A=cosec⁡2A1 + \cot^2 A = \operatorname{cosec}^2 A1+cot2A=cosec2A rearranged — an identity.
Wrong partner: tan pairs with sec. At A = 45°: 1+1=21 + 1 = 21+1=2 and cosec⁡245°=2\operatorname{cosec}^2 45° = 2cosec245°=2 — equal by coincidence; at A = 60°: 1+3=41 + 3 = 41+3=4 but cosec⁡260°=43\operatorname{cosec}^2 60° = \dfrac{4}{3}cosec260°=34​. Not an identity.

Given: four statements. Asked: the one that is not an identity.

Concept used: the three identities and their rearranged forms (Topic 5). Why it applies: three options are rearrangements; one pairs the wrong ratios.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ It is sin⁡2A+cos⁡2A=1\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1sin2A+cos2A=1 rearranged — an identity.
    • (b) ✘ It is 1+tan⁡2A=sec⁡2A1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A1+tan2A=sec2A rearranged — an identity.
    • (c) ✘ It is 1+cot⁡2A=cosec⁡2A1 + \cot^2 A = \operatorname{cosec}^2 A1+cot2A=cosec2A rearranged — an identity.
    • (d) ✔ Wrong partner: tan pairs with sec. At A = 45°: 1+1=21 + 1 = 21+1=2 and cosec⁡245°=2\operatorname{cosec}^2 45° = 2cosec245°=2 — equal by coincidence; at A = 60°: 1+3=41 + 3 = 41+3=4 but cosec⁡260°=43\operatorname{cosec}^2 60° = \dfrac{4}{3}cosec260°=34​. Not an identity.

  2. Check: one counter-example (A = 60°) is enough ✔.

  3. Answer (d)

    Common trap: Testing only at 45°, where (d) happens to work. A single agreeing angle never proves an identity.
P25●●● AdvancedProof · 3 marksOriginal

Challenge (3 moves)

Prove that 1−sin⁡A1+sin⁡A=(sec⁡A−tan⁡A)2\dfrac{1 - \sin A}{1 + \sin A} = (\sec A - \tan A)^21+sinA1−sinA​=(secA−tanA)2.

Full solution

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: start from the RHS (it has more ratios); Move 1, Move 4, Move 5 (Topic 6). Why it applies: changing the RHS to sin and cos produces (1−sin⁡A)2(1 - \sin A)^2(1−sinA)2 over cos⁡2A\cos^2 Acos2A, and cos⁡2A\cos^2 Acos2A factorises.

  1. 1

    Start from the RHS.

    RHS=(sec⁡A−tan⁡A)2\text{RHS} = (\sec A - \tan A)^2RHS=(secA−tanA)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Move 1: change to sin and cos.

    =(1cos⁡A−sin⁡Acos⁡A)2= \left(\dfrac{1}{\cos A} - \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A}\right)^2=(cosA1​−cosAsinA​)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Combine inside the bracket.

    =(1−sin⁡Acos⁡A)2= \left(\dfrac{1 - \sin A}{\cos A}\right)^2=(cosA1−sinA​)2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Square the top and the bottom.

    =(1−sin⁡A)2cos⁡2A= \dfrac{(1 - \sin A)^2}{\cos^2 A}=cos2A(1−sinA)2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Move 4: cos⁡2A=1−sin⁡2A\cos^2 A = 1 - \sin^2 Acos2A=1−sin2A.

    =(1−sin⁡A)21−sin⁡2A= \dfrac{(1 - \sin A)^2}{1 - \sin^2 A}=1−sin2A(1−sinA)2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Move 5: factorise the bottom.

    =(1−sin⁡A)(1−sin⁡A)(1−sin⁡A)(1+sin⁡A)= \dfrac{(1 - \sin A)(1 - \sin A)}{(1 - \sin A)(1 + \sin A)}=(1−sinA)(1+sinA)(1−sinA)(1−sinA)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Cancel (1−sin⁡A)(1 - \sin A)(1−sinA).

    =1−sin⁡A1+sin⁡A=LHS= \dfrac{1 - \sin A}{1 + \sin A} = \text{LHS}=1+sinA1−sinA​=LHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

  8. Hence proved.

    Check: at A = 30°: LHS =1232=13= \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{\dfrac{3}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{3}=23​21​​=31​; RHS =(23−13)2=13= \left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}=(3​2​−3​1​)2=31​ ✔.

  9. Answer Proved (from the RHS to the LHS).

    Common trap: Expanding (sec⁡A−tan⁡A)2(\sec A - \tan A)^2(secA−tanA)2 as sec⁡2A−tan⁡2A=1\sec^2 A - \tan^2 A = 1sec2A−tan2A=1 — the middle term is missing.

P26●●● AdvancedProof · 3 marksOriginal

Challenge (3 moves)

Prove that cos⁡A1−tan⁡A+sin⁡A1−cot⁡A=sin⁡A+cos⁡A\dfrac{\cos A}{1 - \tan A} + \dfrac{\sin A}{1 - \cot A} = \sin A + \cos A1−tanAcosA​+1−cotAsinA​=sinA+cosA.

Full solution

Given: the identity. To prove: LHS = RHS.

Concept used: Move 1 (sin and cos), Move 2 (LCM), Move 5 (a2−b2a^2 - b^2a2−b2). Why it applies: in sin and cos the two denominators become cos⁡A−sin⁡A\cos A - \sin AcosA−sinA and sin⁡A−cos⁡A\sin A - \cos AsinA−cosA.

  1. 1

    Start from the LHS.

    LHS=cos⁡A1−tan⁡A+sin⁡A1−cot⁡A\text{LHS} = \dfrac{\cos A}{1 - \tan A} + \dfrac{\sin A}{1 - \cot A}LHS=1−tanAcosA​+1−cotAsinA​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Move 1: 1−tan⁡A=cos⁡A−sin⁡Acos⁡A1 - \tan A = \dfrac{\cos A - \sin A}{\cos A}1−tanA=cosAcosA−sinA​ and 1−cot⁡A=sin⁡A−cos⁡Asin⁡A1 - \cot A = \dfrac{\sin A - \cos A}{\sin A}1−cotA=sinAsinA−cosA​.

    =cos⁡A  cos⁡A−sin⁡Acos⁡A  +sin⁡A  sin⁡A−cos⁡Asin⁡A  = \dfrac{\cos A}{\;\dfrac{\cos A - \sin A}{\cos A}\;} + \dfrac{\sin A}{\;\dfrac{\sin A - \cos A}{\sin A}\;}=cosAcosA−sinA​cosA​+sinAsinA−cosA​sinA​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Divide by each fraction (multiply by its reciprocal).

    =cos⁡2Acos⁡A−sin⁡A+sin⁡2Asin⁡A−cos⁡A= \dfrac{\cos^2 A}{\cos A - \sin A} + \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\sin A - \cos A}=cosA−sinAcos2A​+sinA−cosAsin2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Write sin⁡A−cos⁡A=−(cos⁡A−sin⁡A)\sin A - \cos A = -(\cos A - \sin A)sinA−cosA=−(cosA−sinA).

    =cos⁡2Acos⁡A−sin⁡A−sin⁡2Acos⁡A−sin⁡A= \dfrac{\cos^2 A}{\cos A - \sin A} - \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\cos A - \sin A}=cosA−sinAcos2A​−cosA−sinAsin2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Move 2: same denominator, combine.

    =cos⁡2A−sin⁡2Acos⁡A−sin⁡A= \dfrac{\cos^2 A - \sin^2 A}{\cos A - \sin A}=cosA−sinAcos2A−sin2A​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Move 5: cos⁡2A−sin⁡2A=(cos⁡A−sin⁡A)(cos⁡A+sin⁡A)\cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = (\cos A - \sin A)(\cos A + \sin A)cos2A−sin2A=(cosA−sinA)(cosA+sinA).

    =(cos⁡A−sin⁡A)(cos⁡A+sin⁡A)cos⁡A−sin⁡A= \dfrac{(\cos A - \sin A)(\cos A + \sin A)}{\cos A - \sin A}=cosA−sinA(cosA−sinA)(cosA+sinA)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Cancel (cos⁡A−sin⁡A)(\cos A - \sin A)(cosA−sinA).

    =cos⁡A+sin⁡A=RHS= \cos A + \sin A = \text{RHS}=cosA+sinA=RHSSwipe to see the whole equation →

    Hence proved. (A ≠ 45°, where 1−tan⁡A=01 - \tan A = 01−tanA=0.)

  8. Check: at A = 60°: LHS =121−3+321−13≈−0.683+2.049=1.366= \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{1 - \sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} \approx -0.683 + 2.049 = 1.366=1−3​21​​+1−3​1​23​​​≈−0.683+2.049=1.366; RHS =1+32≈1.366= \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 1.366=21+3​​≈1.366 ✔.

  9. Answer Proved.

    Common trap: Missing the sign change in step 4, which leaves cos⁡2A+sin⁡2A=1\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1cos2A+sin2A=1 on top and a wrong answer.

P27●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: The school ramp

A school is building a wheelchair ramp to its library entrance. The entrance is 0.55 m above the ground. The first design has a horizontal run of 3 m, so the sloping surface is 3.05 m long. Let θ\thetaθ be the angle the ramp makes with the ground.

(a) Find sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ and tan⁡θ\tan\thetatanθ for the first design. (1)
(b) Accessibility guidelines say tan⁡θ\tan\thetatanθ should not be more than 112\dfrac{1}{12}121​. Does the first design meet the guideline? Justify. (1)
(c) Keeping the same height, find the horizontal run needed so that tan⁡θ=112\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{12}tanθ=121​ exactly. (2)

OR
(c) Find cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ and sec⁡θ\sec\thetasecθ for the first design. (2)

Full solution

Given: rise 0.55 m, run 3 m, slope 3.05 m. Asked: parts (a)–(c).

Concept used: SOH-CAH-TOA with the angle at the ground (Topic 1); a ratio fixes the shape (Topic 3). Why it applies: the ramp, the ground and the wall form a right triangle.

  1. 1

    (a)

    From θ\thetaθ: opposite = rise = 0.55 m, adjacent = run = 3 m, hypotenuse = slope = 3.05 m.

    sin⁡θ=0.553.05=55305=1161,tan⁡θ=0.553=1160\sin\theta = \dfrac{0.55}{3.05} = \dfrac{55}{305} = \dfrac{11}{61}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{0.55}{3} = \dfrac{11}{60}sinθ=3.050.55​=30555​=6111​,tanθ=30.55​=6011​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    (b)

    Compare with 112=560\dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{5}{60}121​=605​: 1160>560\dfrac{11}{60} > \dfrac{5}{60}6011​>605​. So the ramp is too steep; it does not meet the guideline.

  3. 3

    (c)

    We need tan⁡θ=riserun=112\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \dfrac{1}{12}tanθ=runrise​=121​ with rise 0.55 m.

    0.55run=112\dfrac{0.55}{\text{run}} = \dfrac{1}{12}run0.55​=121​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Cross-multiply.

    run=0.55×12=6.6 m\text{run} = 0.55 \times 12 = 6.6 \text{ m}run=0.55×12=6.6 mSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    (c) OR

    cos⁡θ=adjhyp=33.05=6061\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}} = \dfrac{3}{3.05} = \dfrac{60}{61}cosθ=hypadj​=3.053​=6160​, and sec⁡θ=6160\sec\theta = \dfrac{61}{60}secθ=6061​.

  6. Check: 0.552+32=0.3025+9=9.3025=3.0520.55^2 + 3^2 = 0.3025 + 9 = 9.3025 = 3.05^20.552+32=0.3025+9=9.3025=3.052 ✔. 0.556.6=112\dfrac{0.55}{6.6} = \dfrac{1}{12}6.60.55​=121​ ✔.

  7. Answer (a) sin⁡θ=1161\sin\theta = \dfrac{11}{61}sinθ=6111​, tan⁡θ=1160\tan\theta = \dfrac{11}{60}tanθ=6011​ (b) No — 1160>112\dfrac{11}{60} > \dfrac{1}{12}6011​>121​ (c) 6.6 m (c OR) cos⁡θ=6061\cos\theta = \dfrac{60}{61}cosθ=6160​, sec⁡θ=6160\sec\theta = \dfrac{61}{60}secθ=6061​

    Common trap: Using the sloping length 3.05 m as the "run" in (b) or (c). The run is the horizontal distance (adjacent side).

P28●●● AdvancedProof · 3 marksOriginal

If sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \sqrt{2}\cos\thetasinθ+cosθ=2​cosθ, show that cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ\cos\theta - \sin\theta = \sqrt{2}\sin\thetacosθ−sinθ=2​sinθ.

Full solution

Given: sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \sqrt{2}\cos\thetasinθ+cosθ=2​cosθ. To show: cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ\cos\theta - \sin\theta = \sqrt{2}\sin\thetacosθ−sinθ=2​sinθ.

Concept used: this is a given condition, so it may be rearranged like an equation; then rationalise (Topic 2). Why it applies: we can express cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ in terms of sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ from the condition.

  1. 1

    Subtract cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ from both sides of the given equation.

    sin⁡θ=2cos⁡θ−cos⁡θ=(2−1)cos⁡θ\sin\theta = \sqrt{2}\cos\theta - \cos\theta = (\sqrt{2} - 1)\cos\thetasinθ=2​cosθ−cosθ=(2​−1)cosθSwipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Divide both sides by (2−1)(\sqrt{2} - 1)(2​−1).

    cos⁡θ=sin⁡θ2−1\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sqrt{2} - 1}cosθ=2​−1sinθ​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Rationalise with the conjugate (2+1)(\sqrt{2} + 1)(2​+1): (2−1)(2+1)=2−1=1(\sqrt{2} - 1)(\sqrt{2} + 1) = 2 - 1 = 1(2​−1)(2​+1)=2−1=1.

    cos⁡θ=(2+1)sin⁡θ\cos\theta = (\sqrt{2} + 1)\sin\thetacosθ=(2​+1)sinθSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Expand.

    cos⁡θ=2sin⁡θ+sin⁡θ\cos\theta = \sqrt{2}\sin\theta + \sin\thetacosθ=2​sinθ+sinθSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Subtract sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ from both sides.

    cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ\cos\theta - \sin\theta = \sqrt{2}\sin\thetacosθ−sinθ=2​sinθSwipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Hence shown.

    Check: the condition gives tan⁡θ=2−1\tan\theta = \sqrt{2} - 1tanθ=2​−1; then cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ (1−tan⁡θ)=cos⁡θ (2−2)\cos\theta - \sin\theta = \cos\theta\,(1 - \tan\theta) = \cos\theta\,(2 - \sqrt{2})cosθ−sinθ=cosθ(1−tanθ)=cosθ(2−2​) and 2sin⁡θ=2(2−1)cos⁡θ=(2−2)cos⁡θ\sqrt{2}\sin\theta = \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2} - 1)\cos\theta = (2 - \sqrt{2})\cos\theta2​sinθ=2​(2​−1)cosθ=(2−2​)cosθ ✔.

  7. Answer Shown.

    Common trap: Treating this like an identity proof and refusing to rearrange. Here the first line is a given equation, so both sides may be changed.

Given: sec⁡θ+tan⁡θ=3\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 3secθ+tanθ=3. Asked: sec⁡θ\sec\thetasecθ, tan⁡θ\tan\thetatanθ, sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ.

    From the identity, sec⁡θ−tan⁡θ=13\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}secθ−tanθ=31​ … (2), with sec⁡θ+tan⁡θ=3\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 3secθ+tanθ=3 … (1).

  2. 2

    Add (1) and (2).

    2sec⁡θ=3+13=1032\sec\theta = 3 + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{10}{3}2secθ=3+31​=310​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Divide by 2.

    sec⁡θ=53\sec\theta = \dfrac{5}{3}secθ=35​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Subtract (2) from (1).

    2tan⁡θ=3−13=832\tan\theta = 3 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3}2tanθ=3−31​=38​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Divide by 2.

    tan⁡θ=43\tan\theta = \dfrac{4}{3}tanθ=34​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    sin⁡θ=tan⁡θ×cos⁡θ=43×35\sin\theta = \tan\theta \times \cos\theta = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{5}sinθ=tanθ×cosθ=34​×53​.

    sin⁡θ=45\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{5}sinθ=54​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Check: sec⁡θ+tan⁡θ=53+43=3\sec\theta + \tan\theta = \dfrac{5}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} = 3secθ+tanθ=35​+34​=3 ✔; sec⁡2θ−tan⁡2θ=25−169=1\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = \dfrac{25 - 16}{9} = 1sec2θ−tan2θ=925−16​=1 ✔.

  8. Answer sec⁡θ=53\sec\theta = \dfrac{5}{3}secθ=35​, tan⁡θ=43\tan\theta = \dfrac{4}{3}tanθ=34​, sin⁡θ=45\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{5}sinθ=54​

Check: at θ = 60°: 121−32+121+32=12−3+12+3=(2+3)+(2−3)4−3=4\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{1 - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} + \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{1 + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2 - \sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{1}{2 + \sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{(2 + \sqrt{3}) + (2 - \sqrt{3})}{4 - 3} = 41−23​​21​​+1+23​​21​​=2−3​1​+2+3​1​=4−3(2+3​)+(2−3​)​=4 ✔.

    Adjacent =b2−a2= \sqrt{b^2 - a^2}=b2−a2​.

    cos⁡θ=adjhyp=b2−a2b\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{b^2 - a^2}}{b}cosθ=hypadj​=bb2−a2​​.

    Reasoning for each option: (A) ✘ is sec⁡θ\sec\thetasecθ. (B) ✘ is cosec⁡θ\operatorname{cosec}\thetacosecθ. (C) ✔. (D) ✘ is tan⁡θ\tan\thetatanθ.

  3. Check: with a=3a = 3a=3, b=5b = 5b=5: cos⁡θ=45\cos\theta = \dfrac{4}{5}cosθ=54​, and (C) gives 165\dfrac{\sqrt{16}}{5}516​​ ✔.

E6●● StandardMCQ · 1 markNCERT Exemplar Ch 8, Ex 8.1 Q13

If sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ=0\sin\theta - \cos\theta = 0sinθ−cosθ=0, then the value of (sin⁡4θ+cos⁡4θ)(\sin^4\theta + \cos^4\theta)(sin4θ+cos4θ) is

    sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ\sin\theta = \cos\thetasinθ=cosθ gives θ = 45°, so sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ=12\sin\theta = \cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}sinθ=cosθ=2​1​.

    Sum =14+14=12= \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}=41​+41​=21​.

    Reasoning for each option: (C) ✔. (A) ✘ treats sin⁡4θ+cos⁡4θ\sin^4\theta + \cos^4\thetasin4θ+cos4θ like sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\thetasin2θ+cos2θ. (D) ✘ is only one of the two terms. (B) ✘ has no correct route.

    LHS =2tan⁡2θ+tan⁡θ+4tan⁡θ+2=2tan⁡2θ+5tan⁡θ+2= 2\tan^2\theta + \tan\theta + 4\tan\theta + 2 = 2\tan^2\theta + 5\tan\theta + 2=2tan2θ+tanθ+4tanθ+2=2tan2θ+5tanθ+2.

  2. 2

    RHS =5tan⁡θ+1+tan⁡2θ= 5\tan\theta + 1 + \tan^2\theta=5tanθ+1+tan2θ.

  3. 3

    LHS − RHS =tan⁡2θ+1=sec⁡2θ= \tan^2\theta + 1 = \sec^2\theta=tan2θ+1=sec2θ, which is never 0.

Concept used: replace cos⁡2θ\cos^2\thetacos2θ by 1−sin⁡2θ1 - \sin^2\theta1−sin2θ (Topic 5), then read the angle (Topic 4). Why it applies: the equation becomes one in sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ only.

    Divide both sides by 3: sin⁡2θ=1\sin^2\theta = 1sin2θ=1.
